name: DOT Module 3 Hazardous Materials Transportation, Preparing Hazardous Materials for Shipment

slides.title: Preparing Hazardous Materials for Shipment
slides.description: The hazardous materials regulations are aimed at ensuring the safe transportation of hazardous materials. According to the regulations, materials must be in an approved package, marked and labeled correctly and be accompanied by appropriate documentation including safety procedures and information for emergency responders. Module 3 will address the selection of proper packaging, labeling and marking, and the exceptions that may be allowed.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description: Every hazardous material is not compatible with every type of container. Acids and bases may corrode certain materials, and plastics are susceptible to damage from certain chemicals as well. Packaging basically means the receptacle and other components necessary to contain the hazardous materials safely during transportation. Packaging includes fiberboard, aluminum, wood or plastic boxes, metal, plastic, plywood, or fiberboard drums, portable tanks, cargo tanks, and jerricans to name a few. In addition, according to the regulations, authorized packages can be single packagings or combination packagings.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
once you have determined the proper shipping name from Column 2 of the HMT, appropriate packaging information is found in Columns (8A), (8B), and (8C), depending on the hazard class, packing group and quantity being shipped. Recall that Columns (8A)exceptions, (8B)non-bulk packaging and (8C)bulk packaging refer you to appropriate sections of 49 CFR 173.*** (replace the *** with the three numbers listed in column 8, which indicate the section of Part 173 to which you should refer. For example, for acetone, the number listed in Column 8B is 202. This indicates that the non-bulk packaging requirements for acetone are found in 49 CFR 173.202).

If the word "None" appears in Column (8A) then no exceptions apply for that particular hazardous material, and you must refer to either Column (8B) or (8C) depending upon the quantity being shipped. A shipper may choose any of the packagings specified in the appropriate section of 49 CFR Part 173 for that material.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Recall that non bulk packaging means a packaging which has:

  1. maximum capacity of 450 L (119 gallons) or less for liquids
  2. maximum net mass of 400 kg (882 lbs) for solids
  3. a water capacity of 454 kg (1,000 lbs.) or less as a receptacle for a gas

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Let's look at the information in Column 8 and 49 CFR 173 to select packaging. Refer to the TABLE and, in particular, to column 8B. The TABLE entry for "acetone" in column 8B shows ".202" which means packaging information may be found in 49 CFR 173.202. Section 202 applies to "Non-Bulk Packagings for liquid hazardous materials in Packing Group II". The following packagings, among others, are shown in 173.202 under combination packagings and single packagings:

  • For combination packagings;
    • Outer packagings:
      • Fiberboard box: 4G
    • Inner packagings:
      • Glass or earthenware receptacles
      • Plastic receptacles
      • Metal receptacles
  • For single packagings:
    • Steel drum: 1A1 or 1A2
    • Plastic drum: 1H1 or 1H2

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description: A shipper may select either a single packaging, or combination packaging. For combination packaging, a shipper must select both an outer and inner packaging. If a shipper wanted to package acetone in a 55-gallon metal drum he could select a steel, aluminum or other metal drum. In addition, as stated in 173.202, the shipper must conform to the general packaging requirements of Subpart B of part 173. All packaging must be marked with the appropriate UN certification mark such as "UN1A1" for steel drums, as well as the letter (X,Y, or Z) to indicate the packing group performance level and a number indicating the specific gravity or maximum gross weight of the package design. Detailed explanations of markings for non-bulk packagings are found in 49 CFR 178.502 and 178.503. Only UN approved containers are appropriate for shipping hazardous materials.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description: Example: Choose an authorized package forUN 2794, Batteries, wet, filled with acid, electric storage. Look in Column 8b for non-bulk shipments. It refers the user to 49 CFR 173.159. This section covers the requirements for Batteries, wet. Packages must ensure that the batteries are protected to prevent short circuits, and they may not be packed with other materials. 49 CFR 173.159(b) goes on to provide information on which specification packages are authorized. Paragraph (c) indicates non-specification packages which are also authorized for shipments of batteries with no other materials.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Under the performance packaging rules, the containers used for hazardous materials packaging have to meet certain tests in order to be authorized for use. The tests include a drop test, a leakproofness test, and a stacking test, among others. The tests are related to the "degree of danger" of the materials intended to be packaged. They are increasingly severe as the degree of danger increases.

Remember, the degree of danger of a material is referred to as its Packing Group. A drum of "acetone" would represent the medium category of hazard since its flash point is within the range specified in 173.121 and is assigned PGII.

When packaging these materials, letter codes "X", "Y", and "Z" are used to designate the level of testing required. The correct package to be used for hazardous materials is the one(s) authorized in the Hazardous Materials table in Column 8.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Additional considerations that must be addressed when selecting one of the authorized packagings are in 49 CFR 173.24. These are "general requirements for packagings and packages". They include:

  • Compatibility - this must be done even though the packagings are specified in the regulations.
  • Closure - closures must be secure
  • Filling limits - sufficient outage must be left to ensure no leakage occurs.

Also new for 2005 are requirements for overpacks to be marked with the words "Overpack". All required marks and labels on the packaging must be included on the overpack if not readily visible on the inner packaging. This includes the proper shipping name, UN/ID number, the words "Limited Quantity" where applicable and others. This replaces the previous statement "Inner packages comply".

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Packaging Exceptions:

There are exceptions for certain quantities and classes of hazardous materials which permit them to move in non-specification packagings. These are referred to as "limited quantities." and "small quantities".

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description: The exceptions will be shown in Column 8A of the HMT. Each class for which an exception is available is shown in the table below, along with the "maximum" quantity that may be put in one package to qualify for this packaging relief. Refer to the appropriate section of 49 CFR 173 to read the exceptions in more detail.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
For example, when shipping a Class 3 Flammable liquid, you may be able to take advantage of the packaging exceptions. The limited quantity exception for flammable liquids found at 49 CFR 173.150 states that you are not required to meet:

  • the labeling requirements of the hazardous materials regulations (by highway only)
  • the specification packaging requirements, or
  • the placarding requirements,

if you are shipping inner containers holding

  • less than 0.5 liters of a Class 3, PG I material,
  • less than 1.0 liter of a Class 3, PG II material, or
  • less than 5.0 L of a Class 3, PG III material.

In addition, the entire shipment may not exceed 30 kg (66 pounds) gross weight. The shipments must still be marked and still must have the shipping papers and emergency information accompany it to its destination.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
For Class 8 Corrosive materials in Packing Groups II and III, the limited quantity exceptions are found in 49 CFR 173.154 . For these corrosive materials, you may not be required to meet the labeling (for highway only), specification packaging, and placarding requirements if the entire package does not exceed 30 kg (66 pounds) and each inner containers does not exceed the following criteria:

  • For PG II, inner packaging may not exceed 1.0 L (0.3 gallons) for liquids and not over 1.0 kg (2.2 pounds) for solids
  • For PG III, inner packaging may not exceed 4.0 L (1 gallon) for liquids and not over 5.0 kg (11 pounds) for solids

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
The small quantity exceptions apply only to Class 3, Division 4.1, Division 4.2, (PG II, and III), Division 4.3 (PG II and III), Division 5.1 and 5.2, Division 6.1, Class 7, Class 8 and Class 9 materials that also meet the definition of one or more of the above hazard classes.

Small quantity shipments are not subject to any of the requirements when they meet the regulations found in 49 CFR 173.4 which dictate the type of packaging and ID specifications.

In general, to use the small quantity exception, the maximum quantity of hazardous material per inner receptacle is limited to

  • thirty (30) ml (1 ounce) for liquids; and
  • thirty (30) g (1 ounce) for solids.

Division 6.1 and Class 7 radioactives have more detailed requirements in 49 CFR 173.4.

In addition, the entire package may not exceed 29 kg (64 pounds). In order to use the small quantity exception, the outside of the package must be marked with the statement "This package conforms to the conditions and limitations specified in 49 CFR 173.4" .

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
ORM-D (see 49 CFR 173.156)

Hazardous Materials which present a limited hazard during transportation due to their form, quantity and packaging may sometimes be reclassified as (Other Regulated Materials, Domestic) ORM-D. An ORM-D material must be a material that is packaged and distributed in a form intended for retail sales for personal or household use by individuals. It must be a material for which exceptions are provided in Column 8 A of the HMT Table. (Note: The consumer commodity exception applies only to shipments that first meet the requirements of the limited quantity exceptions.)

In most instances ORM-D materials do not require shipping papers. However, if the material is also a hazardous substance, hazardous waste, or marine pollutant, or if the material is to be shipped by air then shipping papers are required.

In addition, ORM-D shipments are excepted from specific packaging and labeling requirements when the material is prepared in a combination packaging system (Outer Package/Inner Package).

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
OUTER PACKAGE REQUIREMENTS

Outer packaging must be “strong”. Although there is no specific testing or construction criteria for how strong these packagings need to be, they must be designed, constructed and closed so that:

  • No identifiable releases occur to the environment.
  • The package system maintains integrity during transport.
  • No mixture of gases or vapors occurs within the package that could reduce the effectiveness of the package.
  • Must be capable of withstanding a drop from four feet high in a position most likely to cause damage without leakage.
  • Each limited quantity package must not exceed 30 kilograms (66 pounds) gross weight.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
INNER PACKAGE REQUIREMENTS

The inner packaging quantity limits vary based on the hazard class and packing group of the material being offered for shipment. Review the limited quantity provision of the specific hazard class.

slides.title: Choosing an Authorized Package
slides.description:
Hazardous Wastes exceptions

Packaging exceptions are provided for hazardous wastes in 49 CFR 173.12. They provide regulatory relief as follows;

  • Use of open-head drums,
  • Use of Lab Packs; and
  • The reuse of previously used packagings.

Certain conditions have to be satisfied in order to take advantage of these exceptions. For example, lab packs may be used:

  • only in highway transportation,
  • only when the waste materials are the same class,
  • only when sufficient absorbent material is placed inside, and
  • only when the gross weight of the drum does not exceed 205 kg.

Previously used packagings may be reused under the conditions specified in paragraph c. This is particularly helpful for shippers who regularly receive hazardous materials as raw materials, then later prepare wastes for disposal in the emptied drums.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
Required Markings and Labels (49 CFR 172.400 172. 301)

Labeling and marking are two of the most important communication requirements in the hazardous materials regulations. The DOT's system of labeling is a visual communication of the "nature" of the hazard contained in the package, and along with package marking, it completes the preparation of the packaging for transportation.

The Labeling requirements are found in 49 CFR 172.400 (Subpart E). The regulations state that, "each person who offers a non-bulk package containing a hazardous material for transportation shall label it, when required, with labels prescribed for the material as specified in the Hazardous Materials Table, column 6." (See 49CFR 172.400). Thus, unless otherwise excepted, (limited quantity, small quantity, etc) a hazardous materials shipment must be labeled according to Column 6 of the HMT. The hazard warning labels are intended to accurately represent the hazard in the package.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description: Other marks on the package should not detract from the visibility of the hazard labels. The required labels must be printed on or affixed to the hazardous materials package near the marked proper shipping name, if the package dimensions are adequate. In addition, the labels must be on a background of contrasting color or have a dotted or solid black line border, and be unobscured by other marks or attachments.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description: Some materials possess more than one hazard and must be labeled accordingly. Multiple labels, if required, must be displayed next to each other. Any hazard class, other than the primary, is called a subsidiary hazard class. Subsidiary hazard class labels are also required. The hazard class number must be displayed in the lower corner of both the primary and subsidiary labels. Additional labeling requirements may be found in 49 CFR 172.402.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
The example given above (Flammable liquid, toxic n.o.s.) is a material with two hazards. The primary hazard and the subsidiary hazard can be determined in the following ways;

  1. The first listed label code in column 6 is the primary hazard of the material; the second listed is the subsidiary. Example: n-Butylamine is a primary Class 3 and a subsidiary Class 8. (See HMT)
  2. The Hazard Precedence Table shown in 173.2a is used when mixtures have more than one hazard of the following classes; 3, 8, Division 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1, and 6.1. For all other classes the order of precedence governs, i.e.,
    • Class 7,
    • Division 2.3,
    • Division 2.1,
    • Division 2.2,
    • Division 6.1, PGI, Inhalation only,
    • Division 4.2 (Pyrophoric),
    • Division 4.1 (Self-reactive),
    • Precedence Table Materials,
    • Combustible liquids,
    • Class 9 (miscellaneous materials).

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
In the example of a material with a proper shipping name of "Flammable liquid, toxic, n.o.s.", the Class 3 label is the primary hazard, and the Class 6.1 label is subsidiary. If the mixture consisted of Toluene (Flammable component) and Trimethylacetyl chloride (Toxic component), the proper shipping name would become "Toxic liquid, flammable, organic, n.o.s." because the toxic component is a Class 6.1, PGI Inhalation Hazard material; it is the primary hazard (see Precedence Table).

The most stringent packing group assigned to a hazard of the material takes precedence over other packing groups; for example, a material meeting Class 3 PGII and Division 6.1 PGI (Oral toxicity) is classified as Class 3, PG I.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
Labeling Exceptions

These are provided throughout the regulations. Some of them are shown in the labeling subpart, Subpart E, Part 172.400a. Others are associated with limited quantities; these are in Part 173 (sections 150 through 156) under the definitions for each hazard class as we saw earlier. In addition, there may be additional exceptions in specific sections.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
For example, 49 CFR 173.159 for Batteries, wet has its own exceptions for marking and labeling. Paragraph (e) states that Electric storage batteries containing electrolyte or corrosive battery fluid are not subject to the other requirements for transportation by highway or rail if all of the following requirements are met:

  • No other hazardous materials may be transported in the same vehicle;
  • The batteries must be loaded or braced so as to prevent damage and short circuits in transit;
  • Any other material loaded in the same vehicle must be blocked, braced, or otherwise secured to prevent contact with or damage to the batteries; and
  • The transport vehicle may not carry material shipped by any person other than the shipper of the batteries.

Be sure to read all of 49 CFR173.159 to ensure you are meeting all of the requirements for proper packaging, marking, labeling, shipping papers, etc.

slides.description:
Each of the labels in the DOT system is specially designed and subject to size and graphic specifications. Here is a carton containing a material with two hazards.

There is no regulatory requirement to put the labels in any specific order; they must only be next to each other.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
Marking Requirements (49 CFR 172.300)

Marking requirements are distinct from labeling requirements. They are more descriptive than the hazard labels and, together with labels and placards, they constitute the "communication" requirements of the HMR.

The HMR state in 49 CFR 172.300 that "each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation shall mark each package, freight container, and transport vehicle containing the hazardous material in the manner required…." To understand the term "marking", look at the definition in 49 CFR 171.8:

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
"'Marking' means a descriptive name, identification number,...or UN marks, or combinations thereof, required... on outer packagings of hazardous materials."

Packages in transportation get handled many times on their way to destination. Markings are very important. They help emergency response personnel to identify the exact nature of the material in case of a spill. Appropriate remedial action can be taken when the markings describe the material fully. Therefore, accurate and consistent descriptions for the various hazardous materials transported must be available at all times.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
Some of the required markings for packagings are listed below. Not all of them will be required for every hazardous materials packaging because which marks are required will depend on what is being shipped and what packaging is used. In general, for non-bulk packagings the following marks are required.

  1. The proper shipping name (172.301(a)(1))from Column 2
  2. The identification number (172.301(a)(1))from Column 4
  3. A technical name, if required (172.301 (b)) For n.o.s. shipments the technical name of at least two components most predominant to the hazard must be marked in parentheses.
  4. An exemption number, if applicable (172.301 (c )
  5. Consignee's or consignor's name and address (172.301 (d)) Other markings that may be required (depending on the hazardous material) include:
  6. Orientation arrows for liquids, single packages with vents, and open cryogenic receptacles(172.312)
  7. The letters "ORM-D" (172.316) for materials classified as ORM-D
  8. The letters "RQ" (172.324) for those materials also meeting the definition of a hazardous substance. In addition, if the hazardous substance is not part of the shipping name, then the name of the hazardous substance or names of the two hazardous substances with the lowest RQ must also be on the package.
  9. The words "TYPE A" or "TYPE B" (Radioactive - 172.310)
  10. The "Marine Pollutant" mark (172.322)
  11. The words "HAZARDOUS WASTE" for RCRA wastes
  12. The words "Inhalation Hazard" must be marked on packages that meet the criteria for Poison-Inhalation hazards or Toxic inhalation hazard.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description: M. Keep Away From Heathandling label must be used in addition to the hazard label on packages containing self-reactive substances in Division 4.1 and Division 5.2 (Organic Peroxides) when transported by air.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description: The markings may be applied in several ways; you may simply print them on the package; you may stencil them on; or you may type them on an adhesive-backed sticker. DOT requires all markings to be durable, in English, and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package, or on a label, tag, or sign. They must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color and unobscured by other labels or attachments that could substantially reduce their effectiveness. Markings must be located near the DOT hazard label. Other markings may be required depending upon the specific hazard of the material.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description: Also included are requirements for overpacks to be marked with the words "Overpack". All required marks and labels on the packaging must be included on the overpack if not readily visible on the inner packaging. This includes the proper shipping name, UN/ID number, the words "Limited Quantity" where applicable and others. This replaces the previous statement "Inner packages comply".

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
ORM-D

Consumer commodities, as defined in 49 CFR 171.8, are eligible for marking exceptions provided in 49 CFR 173.150-173.156. Each non-bulk packaging containing a material classed as ORM-D must be marked immediately following or below the proper shipping name with the designation shown. This marking is used when the product is eligible to be re-classed as a "consumer commodity" because of the quantity in the inner packaging. If a material has been reclassed as an ORM-D material, the only marking requirement is the proper shipping name and the ORM-D symbol ("ORM-D" in a black rectangular box). That marking is the offeror's certification that the package meets the requirements (§172.316).

In addition, shipments of ORM-D materials are not subject to the shipping paper requirements of Subpart C of Part 172 of 49 CFR unless the material meets the definition of a hazardous substance, a hazardous waste, or a marine pollutant or unless offered or intended for transportation by aircraft.

slides.title: Required Markings and Labels
slides.description:
Identification Numbers

For large quantities of a single hazardous material in non bulk packages (greater than 4,000 kg from the same facility), the transit vehicles containing the hazardous material must be marked on each side and each end as with theidentification numberspecified for the hazardous material in the 172.101 Table, if the vehicle contains no other hazardous material. This requirement is subject to certain limitations in 173.301.

If you are offering hazardous materials for transportation, be sure that they are properly marked and labeled according to the regulations. For example, bulk packaging containing regulated medical waste must be marked with a biohazard marking, conforming to 29 CFR 1910.1030(g)(1)(i) (Note: this is a OSHA 29 CFR requirement, not a DOT requirement).
